steps: The addition rule is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); the overlap must be subtracted because it is counted in both totals.

referenceExample.prompt: 30 people; 18 do A, 14 do B, 7 do both. Find P(A or B).

commonErrors.observed: Added the two totals without subtracting the overlap.
commonErrors.likelyCause: The people doing both activities were counted twice.
commonErrors.remediation: Draw the two-circle diagram and label each region separately before adding.

steps: "At least one success" is the complement of "no successes at all", which is easier to compute directly.
The probability of failure on one trial is 3/4.
Because the trials are independent, the probability of two failures is (3/4)² = 9/16.

referenceExample.prompt: P(success) = 1/3 per trial, two trials. P(at least one)?

commonErrors.likelyCause: The two trials were treated as mutually exclusive rather than independent.
commonErrors.remediation: Test the shortcut with a probability above 1/2; doubling produces a value greater than 1, which is impossible.

steps: The condition "given group X" restricts attention to group X only.

referenceExample.prompt: Group X: 12 successes, 8 failures. Find P(success | X).

commonErrors.likelyCause: The joint probability was computed instead of the conditional one.
commonErrors.remediation: Circle the row or column the condition names, and take the denominator only from inside it.

answers.answer: No; P(A and B) differs from P(A)·P(B).

steps: Two events are independent exactly when P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). This is a numerical test, not a description of the events.
29/100 differs from 24/100, so A and B are not independent.
solutionReasoning.answer: No; P(A and B) differs from P(A)·P(B).

referenceExample.prompt: P(A) = 5/10, P(B) = 4/10, P(A and B) = 20/100. Independent?

commonErrors.observed: Concluded independence because the events could occur together.
commonErrors.likelyCause: Independence was confused with being non-mutually-exclusive.
commonErrors.remediation: Independence is a numerical condition; always multiply the two probabilities and compare.
